title: How many labeled jailbreak examples are needed to train a reliable linear probe detector?

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: quantifying the minimum labeled data requirement sets realistic expectations for practitioners and informs annotation effort. Very low requirements would further support the 'almost free' claim; high requirements would qualify it. Directly actionable for deployment decisions.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Learning curve analysis (train on subsets of increasing size, plot AUROC) is a standard ML evaluation technique. Uses logistic regression on pre-existing benchmark data. A motivated beginner with basic Python/ML skills can execute this with minimal ramp-up.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Tightly scoped: vary dataset size (6 sizes), train probe, plot AUROC with confidence intervals from 5 seeds. Single precise experiment with an obvious deliverable (learning curve plot and data efficiency knee). Can go from start to meaningful result in a few hours.

novelty.reasoning: While linear probes for jailbreak detection have been studied (EMNLP 2025 Findings, BlackboxNLP 2025), and sample efficiency is discussed tangentially (JBShield needs only 30 calibration samples), no published work systematically constructs a learning curve showing AUROC vs training set size for activation-based linear probe jailbreak detectors. The data efficiency question is practical and deployment-critical. PromptScreen evaluated TF-IDF classifiers but not activation-based probes. The proposed 6-point learning curve with confidence intervals from 5 seeds is a clean experiment not directly available in the literature.
